unit.title: Security: the basics
unit.description: Vulnerabilities, attack surface, confidentiality, integrity, availability, least privilege, defense in depth, updates

cards.definition: A weakness in a site or its setup that an attacker can use to do something they should not be able to do.
cards.example: A login form that accepts unlimited password guesses.

cards.definition: Everything an attacker can reach and try: pages, forms, APIs, open ports, plugins, admin panels.
cards.example: An old, forgotten test page still online widens it.

cards.definition: The three goals of security: data is seen only by the right people, changed only by the right people, and reachable when needed.
cards.example: A leak breaks confidentiality, a tampered price breaks integrity, an outage breaks availability.

cards.definition: Every person, program and account gets only the rights it needs for its job, nothing more.
cards.example: The newsletter tool can read emails of subscribers, not delete orders.

cards.definition: Stacking several independent protections so that when one fails, another still stops the attacker.
cards.example: Hashed passwords, plus two-factor login, plus alerts on strange logins.

cards.definition: Anything coming from the browser can be modified by the user, so every check that matters must be done again on the server.
cards.example: A price sent by the page is ignored; the server reads the price from the database.

cards.definition: A new version that fixes a known vulnerability; once it is public, attackers scan for sites that have not installed it.
cards.example: A WordPress plugin patch is published and bots start testing sites the same week.

choices: A weakness an attacker can use
A virus that is already on the server
exercises.explain: A vulnerability is the open door. An exploit is the method that walks through it; a firewall or a strong password are protections.

exercises.prompt: An attacker changes the prices in your shop database. Which goal of security is broken?
exercises.explain: Integrity means data is only changed by the right people. Nothing leaked and the site is up, but the data can no longer be trusted.

exercises.prompt: The email addresses of your customers end up on a public forum. Which goal is broken?
exercises.explain: Confidentiality means only the right people can see the data. A leak is the textbook breach of it.

exercises.prompt: Your site goes down under a flood of fake requests (a DDoS). Which goal is broken?
exercises.explain: Availability means the service is reachable when needed. Nothing was stolen or changed, but real users cannot use the site.

exercises.prompt: Checking a form field only with JavaScript in the browser is enough to protect the server.
exercises.explain: False: the user can switch off JavaScript or send requests directly. Browser checks are for comfort; the server must check again.

exercises.prompt: A marketing intern needs to read the site statistics. Which access should they get?
choices: Admin access, to avoid asking later
exercises.explain: Least privilege limits the damage of a mistake, a stolen account or a lost laptop.

exercises.prompt: Passwords are already hashed. Why add two-factor login on top?
choices: If one layer fails, another still stops the attacker
It makes the site load faster
The law requires two-factor login only
exercises.explain: Defense in depth: a password can be phished or reused; the second factor still blocks the login.

exercises.prompt: Which action reduces the attack surface of your site?
choices: Removing an unused admin page and old plugins
Opening more ports on the server
Publishing a debug page for the team
exercises.explain: Less code and fewer entry points online means fewer places to attack.

exercises.prompt: Most attacks on small sites come from automated bots scanning for known flaws, not from a hacker targeting you personally.
exercises.explain: True: bots test millions of sites for known weaknesses. Being small does not protect you; being up to date does.

exercises.prompt: A security update is released for a plugin your site uses. Best move?
choices: Install it quickly, after a short test
Wait a year to see if it is stable
Ignore it while the site still works
Delete your backups to save space
exercises.explain: Once a fix is public, attackers know where to look. Patch fast, with a backup and a quick check.
